title: We Can’t Predict What Will Happen on Election Day. But We’ll Be Here to Cover It.
author: Stephen Engelberg
content:
This has been a midterm election cycle unlike any other. Wealthy donors [spent
staggering sums](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/12/us/politics/elon-musk-
midterms.html). Both parties moved to [redraw congressional district
lines](https://apnews.com/projects/2026-elections-redistricting-maps/).
President Donald Trump and his allies relentlessly questioned whether the
[results could be
trusted](https://www.washingtonpost.com/elections/2026/10/27/trump-declines-
unconditionally-accept-midterm-results/) even before a single ballot was
counted. At Trump’s direction, the Justice Department [filed a
lawsuit](https://apnews.com/article/alaska-senate-race-sullivan-name-lawsuit-
certification-d8f4a3c7b5247cc427a05f796d7c0d82) that said the federal
government would contest any outcome in which Sen. Dan Sullivan, the
Republican incumbent in Alaska, was not victorious.

Newsrooms, including ours, have tried to plan how we will cover an election in
which the losing side refuses to accept the will of the voters. Was the Alaska
lawsuit a single data point or a harbinger?

As we prepare to write about Nov. 3 and beyond, we find ourselves in the
uncomfortable position of trying to game out what might happen in the future —
not our strong suit. The record shows that journalists are pretty good at
telling readers what happened, particularly if we have some time and some data
to sift through, and much less good at forecasting the future.

* * *

### Help Us Report on Key Election Issues

ProPublica’s reporters are on the lookout for what’s going right and what
isn’t. We’re monitoring **voter suppression** and interference, **election
observers** and**** poll watchers, **extremism** tied to the election,
and**ICE activity** at the polls. Have you seen something?

[Send Us a Tip](https://www.propublica.org/tips/)

* * *

And yet we have to plan. Over the past few weeks we have prepared our
reporters and editors to cover every scenario we can imagine. None of us have
forgotten the chaos of 2020 when Trump was urged by advisers to send the
military to [seize voting
machines](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/01/11/us/trump-voting-
machines-2020-election.html) in states he had lost. The [Jan. 6, 2021, attack
on the Capitol](https://www.propublica.org/topics/jan-6) as lawmakers gathered
to certify Joe Biden’s victory underscored the sense that literally anything
was possible in the aftermath of elections.

We will have reporters on the ground in 11 key states covering voting, with
even more in Washington, D.C., and others on standby. Our reporters have
detailed [what experts will be
watching](https://www.propublica.org/article/five-voting-disruptions-midterm-
election). But elections are no longer confined to Election Day (early voting
and voting by mail constitute a huge share of the electorate). And our plans
for covering voting stretch back many months.

Over the past year, we’ve tried to use the techniques of accountability
journalism to add new facts to this pivotal moment in American history.

We have focused considerable attention on the mechanics of elections, a once-
arcane issue that has become a central aspect of the MAGA movement’s argument
that Trump’s [2020 loss was “rigged”](https://www.propublica.org/article/big-
lie-trump-stolen-election-inside-creation) by his opponents. We examined how
the Trump administration depleted [the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure
Security Agency](https://www.propublica.org/article/cisa-election-security-
donald-trump), the arm of the federal government charged with safeguarding
election systems. We discovered that Department of Homeland Security officials
had asked CISA to obtain a voting machine and hack it without informing the
manufacturer of any vulnerabilities found. The plan wasn’t acted on, but its
existence made CISA employees fear they were being asked to take part in
political interference. CISA and DHS didn’t respond to our questions, but a
White House spokesperson said Trump “has done more than any other President to
ensure we have free and fair elections.”

Another story looked at how delays resulting from the [U.S. Postal Service’s
cost-cutting measures endangered the validity of mail-in ballots in rural
counties](https://www.propublica.org/article/mail-ballot-delays-postal-
service-midterms), typically Republican strongholds, during this year’s
primaries. The Postal Service said such delays are less likely in the general
election.

One of our most detailed election stories traced [the career of Cleta
Mitchell](https://www.propublica.org/article/cleta-mitchell-elections-trump),
a lawyer who spearheaded the legal attacks on the 2020 results. Mitchell leads
a coalition of what she calls “election believers” — people who scour the
voting results for errors that they believe point to larger conspiracies.
Changes she’d hoped Trump could push through before the midterms, such as
compelling states to turn over confidential voter information to the Justice
Department, have been [blocked by the
courts](https://projects.propublica.org/trump-doj-voter-data-lawsuits/). But
she has nonetheless become the voice of a well-funded national movement, one
which has the president’s ear. When Trump is weighing what to do in the
aftermath of this week’s vote, our reporting strongly suggests that Mitchell
will be among the people he listens to.

We asked to speak with Mitchell multiple times. She declined but told us in an
email: “​​​​What we focus on is making sure the election process is accurate,
transparent, and honest. The ONLY steps I’ve urged the Administration to take
are those that will give the voters — ALL voters — confidence that the
outcomes are correct.” A White House spokesperson said she has no official
role in election policy but is an effective private advocate.

We have also spent time doing the traditional work of investigative reporting,
looking closely at candidates’ records in public office. A newsroom like ours
can’t cover every race, so we focus our resources on areas where we have
particular expertise.

Our team in Texas has covered state Attorney General Ken Paxton for years, and
we kept our focus once he announced he would run for the U.S. Senate. One
story looked at his travels, revealing that only 1 in 6 of his nearly 1,000
out-of-state trips were linked to his official duties. [Texas taxpayers paid
$3.3 million for Paxton’s security detail to accompany
him.](https://www.propublica.org/article/ken-paxton-travel-security-costs)
(Paxton didn’t answer our questions, but his office said he “faced numerous
security threats.”) That has become an issue in the Senate campaign.

Another opportunity arose from an investigation that was seemingly not related
to the midterms: our examination of the Trump administration’s handling of the
Justice Department. We began many months ago to look for promising cases that
had been dropped and found out the FBI had been looking into pay-to-play
allegations involving prominent Democratic and Republican members of Congress.
The case included a bipartisan list of political figures such as [Susan
Collins](https://www.propublica.org/article/fbi-susan-collins-navatek-
campaign-donations-investigation), the Republican senator from Maine running
in a closely contested race this year, and [James
Clyburn](https://www.propublica.org/article/navatek-lindsey-graham-jim-
clyburn-fbi-anti-corruption-bribery), a leading Democratic representative from
South Carolina who’s also on the ballot this year.

Our [first story revealed](https://www.propublica.org/article/fbi-susan-
collins-navatek-campaign-donations-investigation) that Collins helped a
little-known defense contractor win millions in federal contracts while the
company’s CEO helped bankroll her 2020 reelection effort through a donation
made via a shell company. Our [second story
revealed](https://www.propublica.org/article/navatek-lindsey-graham-jim-
clyburn-fbi-anti-corruption-bribery) that the FBI was looking into
interactions that Clyburn and Sen. Lindsey Graham, who died in July, had with
the same contractor. Collins has denied all wrongdoing. “A donation would
never cause Congressman Clyburn to increase his support for the donor’s
request,” Clyburn’s office said. Graham’s communications director wrote that
“any allegations of quid-pro-quo behavior … are simply false.” The FBI stopped
examining the allegations after Trump purged the bureau. Our coverage likewise
has become an issue in the Maine race.

We stand at a moment of uncertainty in our history as a democracy. Trump has
made his willingness to smear news organizations an essential aspect of his
appeal. He routinely insults reporters to their face and has [attempted to ban
some outlets from the White
House](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/20/us/politics/trump-white-house-
media.html) and [Air Force
One](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-28/cnn-adds-air-force-
one-access-to-suit-over-trump-white-house-ban) because he didn’t like the
stories they wrote about him. He has diverted hundreds of federal agents from
their jobs fighting drug cartels and organized crime to search for evidence
that noncitizens have illegally voted in federal elections. Hardly [any were
found](https://www.propublica.org/article/noncitizen-voting-trump-homeland-
security-investigations).

I’m deeply reluctant to make any predictions about how all this will end.
ProPublica prepared for an array of dire scenarios in November of 2024 that
might arise from a close election. None of them came to pass as Trump
decisively prevailed. A federal judge [dismissed the Justice Department’s
lawsuit to block the Alaska Senate race
results](https://www.npr.org/2026/11/01/nx-s1-6023766/doj-alaska-lawsuit-
senate-race-dan-sullivan) over the weekend, and the Trump administration’s
plans to appeal stand on shaky legal ground.

The one thing I know for certain is that we will keep digging into the story
of what really happened in this election, whoever wins.

The post [We Can’t Predict What Will Happen on Election Day. But We’ll Be Here
to Cover It.](https://www.propublica.org/article/propublica-
approach-2026-midterm-elections) appeared first on
[ProPublica](https://www.propublica.org).
